cards.title: What changes when the same oscillator becomes heavier or stiffer?
cards.explain: The comparison changes **mass** in one system and **stiffness** in another while retaining a reference oscillator. Watching the cycles over the same interval separates a change in frequency from a change in the size of the movement.
cards.outcome: The heavier system completes fewer cycles, while the stiffer system completes more. **More inertia slows reversal, and stronger restoring force speeds it up**.
cards.interpret: The useful prediction specifies what changed and what was held constant. Making the mass move farther is an amplitude change and is not itself the frequency comparison being tested.

cards.title: Why do two connected masses have a slower pattern and a faster one?
cards.explain: Two equal masses are connected between fixed supports. One pattern moves them together, another moves them in opposite directions, and a further display combines the two patterns.
cards.outcome: The opposing pattern stretches the middle connection more strongly and has the higher frequency. **The mixture contains both modes**, even though its combined motion is not one simple normal mode.
cards.interpret: A mode describes coordinated motion of the whole system. The two masses do not each own a separate independent frequency while vibrating in one normal mode.

cards.title: Would making the middle mass heavier slow every mode?
cards.explain: The three-mass pattern has a middle mass that moves in Modes 1 and 3 but remains stationary in Mode 2. The proposed change adds mass only at that middle position.
cards.outcome: **Modes 1 and 3 shift downward**, while Mode 2 is unchanged in the ideal symmetric system. Extra inertia matters only where the mode has motion.
cards.interpret: This is a directional application of the mode patterns, not a newly measured result. It answers the Exam 2 review’s local-mass question without inferring effects from arbitrary drawing amplitudes.

cards.title: How can one local change push two mode frequencies in opposite directions?
cards.explain: The same marked location is strongly moving in one string mode and stationary but strongly deformed in another. The comparison increases mass and stiffness at that location together.
cards.outcome: The mode dominated by local motion shifts downward because of the added mass. The mode dominated by local deformation shifts upward because of the added stiffness.
cards.interpret: **Location within each mode determines which effect matters**. Treating the simultaneous changes as an automatic cancellation loses the spatial information that makes the prediction possible.

cards.title: Does a recorded periodic voice have the predicted harmonic spacing?
cards.explain: A physical account of the voice predicts regularly spaced harmonics. Recording a sustained voiced sound and inspecting a spectrum provides a measurable comparison with that prediction.
cards.outcome: The transcript describes checking the lowest harmonic and a neighboring harmonic, finding the expected spacing. The relevant result is **regular spacing tied to the periodic source**, rather than the memorization of one speaker’s measured pitch.
cards.interpret: The measurement connects theory with an observable pattern. It supports the predicted relationship while leaving the original source and measurement context available for inspection.

cards.title: Why do changing endpoint constraints change the allowed frequency series?
cards.explain: The fixed-at-both-ends string must remain still at both ends. The fixed–free example must remain still at one end and reach maximal displacement at the other.
cards.outcome: Whole numbers of half-waves fit the first arrangement. **Odd numbers of quarter-waves** fit the second arrangement, producing the ideal odd-multiple series.
cards.interpret: The endpoint conditions determine which patterns are allowed. The comparison concerns the ideal source models, with their own tuning, rather than a claim that every real building has perfectly odd-spaced resonances.

cards.title: Why does moving a constriction change the relationship between F1 and F2?
cards.explain: The three configurations place loading near the lips, near the front constriction for /i/, or nearer the /a/ constriction. The local motion and compression patterns are checked separately for the first two modes.
cards.outcome: **/u/ lowers both formants, /i/ lowers F1 and raises F2, and /a/ raises F1 and lowers F2** in the illustrated models. The same kind of local physical change can therefore have different consequences at different positions.
cards.interpret: The explanation is the relationship between the constriction and the mode pattern. A memorized list of directions is less useful than knowing which mode moves or compresses at the narrowed location.

cards.title: Can one harmonic source acquire different vowel qualities?
cards.explain: The source supplies regularly spaced harmonic peaks. Different tract filters favor different frequency regions while the source spacing can remain the same.
cards.outcome: The relative harmonic heights change around the **formant resonances**, producing different envelopes for the vowels. The filter does not have to move every harmonic frequency to change the sound’s quality.
cards.interpret: This separates the acoustic role of the vocal folds from the role of the tract. Pitch depends on source periodicity, while vowel quality depends strongly on the resonant shaping of that source.

cards.title: Why is the same formant pattern easier to read with a lower-pitched source?
cards.explain: The display applies comparable vowel filters to source rows with different F0 values. A higher F0 leaves fewer harmonic peaks within the same frequency window.
cards.outcome: Closely spaced harmonics trace the envelope more densely. **Sparse harmonics can miss a resonance region**, making the intended vowel pattern less clear.
cards.interpret: A less visible peak does not establish that the tract stopped having that resonance. The comparison separates the filter’s response from how densely the source samples it.

cards.title: How does a sequence of spectra become a picture of a changing vowel?
cards.explain: Each spectrum gives the frequency content of a short time window. Placing those windows in time order and mapping amplitude to darkness produces the spectrogram.
cards.outcome: The formant bands become trajectories through time. In the /i/ to /a/ comparison, **F1 rises while F2 falls** toward the new configuration.
cards.interpret: The resulting display preserves both frequency relationships and their timing. It adds information that cannot be recovered from a single isolated spectrum.

cards.title: Why can a consonant from ma be heard as na after splicing?
cards.explain: A consonant fragment is taken from ma and joined to the vowel portion of na. The fragments provide conflicting information about the identity of the preceding consonant.
cards.outcome: The transcript describes the resulting percept as **na**. The vowel’s formant transition carries information associated with /n/ and can dominate the decision.
cards.interpret: Listeners use context extending into the following vowel. The result argues against treating recognition as an independent decision on every tiny slice of sound.

cards.title: What does an untrained network do with an /i/-like input?
cards.explain: The two input formants fit the /i/-like category dean, but the current weights are not yet useful. A forward pass computes the category distribution from those weights.
cards.outcome: The displayed decision favors **done rather than dean**. The distribution can satisfy the probability rules while assigning its greatest support to the wrong category.
cards.interpret: A valid output format is different from an accurate classification. The target supplies the desired category so the network’s error can guide later learning.

cards.title: Does inserting sigmoid leave the final prediction unchanged?
cards.explain: The formant inputs stay fixed while hidden weighted sums are passed through sigmoid. Each transformed hidden value becomes the input used by the following layer.
cards.outcome: The downstream activations and final output distribution change. **Changing the processing rule is enough to change the decision**, even before any training update occurs.
cards.interpret: This comparison does not establish that sigmoid by itself makes the classifier correct. It separates a nonlinear transformation of the forward computation from learning the weights.

cards.title: How much of the vowel distinction does the displayed linear training run learn?
cards.explain: The F1–F2 data contain overlapping vowel categories. The supplied curve tracks training accuracy as the linear network’s parameters are updated repeatedly.
cards.outcome: Accuracy rises above the roughly one-in-five baseline and levels off at **44.95 percent** in the displayed run. The source labels this curve as an equivalent NumPy reference run rather than executed PyTorch output.
cards.interpret: The run learns useful distinctions but still makes many training errors. Its final percentage describes this dataset, architecture and procedure, not a general ceiling on vowel recognition.

cards.title: Do different random starting weights force different final accuracies?
cards.explain: Ten runs use the same displayed training setup with different initial parameter values. Their accuracy curves can be compared over the same update range.
cards.outcome: The paths differ but all displayed runs end at **44.95 percent training accuracy**. Initial differences therefore do not force different final proportions correct in this setup.
cards.interpret: Repeated outcomes strengthen the observation for the supplied experiment. They do not guarantee that every initialization, implementation or new dataset will produce that result.

cards.title: What can the next-letter game reveal about English knowledge?
cards.explain: A beginning such as sp is supplied and the next letter must continue a possible word. Some beginnings permit many choices, while others strongly limit what can follow.
cards.outcome: The accepted continuations track the illustrated onset and spelling restrictions. **A good prediction requires sensitivity to the pattern**, even if no explicit verbal rule was given.
cards.interpret: The exercise motivates learning from completion. It is not a measured accuracy report for a trained language model, and its spelling examples should not be confused with a complete phonetic transcription.

contrasts.title: Mass and stiffness change frequency in opposite directions.

left.text: **Mass resists changes in motion**. Increasing the moving mass makes acceleration and reversal slower when the restoring stiffness stays fixed.

right.text: **Stiffness determines the restoring response to displacement**. Increasing it gives a stronger return force for the same displacement when mass stays fixed.

paragraphs: The first change lowers frequency, while the second raises it. A prediction about both changing together needs their relative effects and, in a distributed system, their locations.
A heavy mass takes longer to reverse, while a stronger spring reverses the same mass more quickly. Large movement alone describes amplitude and does not decide which system cycles faster.

contrasts.title: A stationary point can have strong spring action.

left.text: A **displacement node stays still** in that mode. Neighboring motion can nevertheless produce strong local deformation or compression.

right.text: A **displacement antinode has greatest motion**. In the illustrated standing-wave model, local deformation is least there.

paragraphs: Added mass has little or no effect at an exact displacement node because that location contributes no motion. Added stiffness matters where the mode has deformation, so a still point can remain important.
The same marked position can be a node in one mode and an antinode in another. Reading the two patterns separately explains why the same perturbation can produce opposite changes.

contrasts.title: Air motion and air compression are different measurements.

left.text: **Displacement describes how far a particle moves from its resting position**. Strong displacement indicates substantial back-and-forth motion.

right.text: **Compression describes changes in how closely particles are packed**. It can be strong near a place whose own particle displacement is small.

paragraphs: The displacement of one particle and the changing separation between neighboring particles are different quantities. A constriction’s effect depends on which pattern dominates for the mode at that location.
For /i/, the front constriction acts where Mode 1 mainly moves but Mode 2 mainly compresses. The corresponding shifts are F1 downward and F2 upward.

contrasts.title: One mode is an organized pattern, while a mixture combines patterns.

left.text: A **normal mode** has a coordinated spatial pattern and its own characteristic frequency. The pattern describes the system as a whole.

right.text: A **mixture** adds contributions from several normal modes. Its visible movement can be more complicated than any component pattern.

paragraphs: Seeing complex motion does not establish another independent normal mode. A spectrum can reveal frequencies whose simultaneous contributions make up the combined movement.
The lower row of the two-mass demonstration combines its two modes. It should not be assigned one of the two mode frequencies as if it contained only that mode.

contrasts.title: The allowed frequency series follows the endpoint constraints.

left.text: Both endpoints must have **zero displacement**. The ideal uniform string fits whole numbers of half-waves, giving whole-number harmonics.

right.term: One fixed end and one free end
right.text: One endpoint is still while the other has **greatest displacement**. The ideal model fits odd numbers of quarter-waves.

paragraphs: A whole-number sequence and an odd-number sequence follow from different permitted spatial patterns. Counting the wave pieces explains the series instead of leaving it as a rule to memorize.
A 200 Hz fixed-at-both-ends string has a fifth mode at 1,000 Hz. A neutral fixed–free tube with a 500 Hz first resonance has its next resonance at 1,500 Hz.

contrasts.title: Harmonics belong to the source, while formants belong to the filter.

left.text: **Harmonics are whole-number multiples of the source’s fundamental frequency**. Their spacing follows how quickly the source repeats.

right.text: **Formants are resonances of the vocal tract**. Their locations depend strongly on the tract’s configuration.

paragraphs: The filter changes the relative strengths of the available source harmonics. A formant does not have to coincide exactly with a harmonic, and its number is not the number of that harmonic.
Changing from /i/ to /a/ can move the formant pattern while preserving F0. Raising F0 can spread the harmonics apart while the intended vowel filter stays similar.

contrasts.title: Pitch and vowel quality can change independently.

left.text: The periodic voiced source’s **F0** is closely related to pitch. Faster vocal-fold repetition produces wider harmonic spacing.

right.text: The tract’s **formant pattern** contributes strongly to vowel identity. Moving the tongue or lips changes that pattern.

paragraphs: A higher-pitched /i/ is not automatically /a/. However, sparse high-F0 harmonics can make the resonance pattern harder to identify, so independence of the mechanisms does not imply perfect perceptual separation.
A singer can keep the intended vowel while changing the note. At very high pitches, the small number of harmonics near a formant can make that vowel less clear.

contrasts.title: The /i/ and /a/ constrictions reverse the two dominant effects.

left.text: The front constriction loads a moving region of Mode 1 and a compressing region of Mode 2. **F1 falls and F2 rises**.

right.text: The more posterior constriction catches the two modes in the opposite local roles. **F1 rises and F2 falls**.

paragraphs: The physical changes produced by narrowing are not arbitrary for each vowel. Their consequences differ because the same kinds of changes occur at different places within the mode patterns.
A transition from /i/ toward /a/ should bring the first two formant bands closer together. The explanation comes from the reversal of the dominant inertial and stiffness effects.

contrasts.title: Two high vowels can have different second formants.

left.text: Loading near the lips acts on strong motion in both first modes. **Both F1 and F2 fall** in the illustrated comparison.

right.text: A front constriction affects motion in the first mode and compression in the second. **F1 falls while F2 rises**.

paragraphs: Calling both vowels high describes tongue height and does not establish the same acoustic pattern. Lip shape and the location of narrowing affect the second mode differently.
The vowels in dune and dean share a high-vowel description but occupy different parts of an F1–F2 comparison. The second formant helps separate their acoustic patterns.

contrasts.title: A spectrum is a snapshot, while a spectrogram retains change over time.

left.text: A **spectrum** gives frequency content within one analysis window. Frequency runs horizontally and height represents amplitude.

right.text: A **spectrogram** places analysis windows in time order. Frequency runs vertically and darkness represents amplitude.

paragraphs: The displays encode related information with different visual arrangements. A high point in a spectrum means strong amplitude, while a high location in a spectrogram means high frequency.
A changing vowel can be followed as moving formant bands in the spectrogram. One spectrum cannot tell whether those resonances had just risen or were about to fall.

contrasts.title: An input describes the observation, while a target identifies its correct category.

left.text: The **input row** contains the measured F1 and F2 values. Those measurements are what the network receives to classify the vowel.

right.text: The **target row** places one in the correct vowel’s output column and zeros in the others. It supplies the desired answer for training.

paragraphs: The target is not another measured formant and does not replace the input. Its role is to reveal the mismatch between the network’s prediction and the known identity.
An /i/-like formant row belongs with the dean target. Shuffling one table without the other would teach incorrect associations.

contrasts.title: A valid distribution can still make the wrong decision.

left.text: A **valid probability distribution** has nonnegative entries that sum to one. Those conditions describe its mathematical form.

right.text: A **correct classification** favors the actual category for the input. Accuracy concerns the connection between the prediction and the known identity.

paragraphs: Probability rules alone cannot establish that the weights have learned useful categories. A distribution over the wrong answer can be perfectly well formed.
The displayed untrained network favors done for an input whose target is dean. That is a classification error rather than a failure of the entries to add to one.

contrasts.title: An activation changes with the input, while a weight controls a connection.

left.text: An **activation** is a value produced or supplied during processing. It changes as the input and upstream computations change.

right.text: A **weight** determines how a connection contributes to a receiving neuron. It is a learned parameter used during a forward pass.

paragraphs: A large activation is not the same as a large learned connection. The receiving neuron combines both by multiplying the input activation by its connection weight.
Changing F1 can change hidden activations without changing any weights. A training update changes weights and can therefore change how a later input is processed.

contrasts.title: Inference uses the weights, while learning changes them.

left.text: **Inference** computes a decision using the current weights. It can be performed with useful or untrained parameters.

right.text: **Learning** uses feedback to improve the parameters. It requires a comparison with a target or another training objective.

paragraphs: A forward pass is needed to discover the network’s current mistake. Repeating it with unchanged inputs and weights does not itself perform the correction.
The untrained network already produces a full distribution. Training matters because the target and error guide changes in the connections behind that distribution.

contrasts.title: Backpropagation and SGD perform different parts of an update.

left.text: **Backpropagation computes gradients** by carrying error information through the dependent computations in reverse order.

right.text: **SGD applies parameter changes** using the gradients and a learning rate. It is the optimizer rather than the reverse calculation itself.

paragraphs: The reverse calculation reuses downstream work, connecting it to dynamic programming. The optimizer then decides how far to move along the supplied correction direction.
loss.backward() prepares gradients, while the optimizer’s step applies them. Describing both as the same operation leaves out the difference between calculating a correction and performing it.

contrasts.title: A final connection has a shorter route to the error than an early connection.

left.text: A final-layer weight affects the output through relatively few computations. Its influence is comparatively direct.

right.text: An early weight changes intermediate activations that pass through more connections. Its final influence depends on those downstream pathways.

paragraphs: This dependency explains the order of the backward calculation. Reusing solved downstream derivatives makes the earlier problem manageable without guessing at each connection’s isolated effect.
A positive input to a direct output weight gives a clear local sign relationship. The sign of an early connection alone does not establish the sign of its effect on every final category.

contrasts.title: Hidden layers process evidence, while output positions name the candidate categories.

left.text: **Hidden layers** transform representations between the supplied input and final decision. Their neurons are not extra category labels.

right.text: The **output layer** provides values corresponding to the defined answer categories. In the illustrated vowel network it has five positions.

paragraphs: Four processing layers can therefore contain only three hidden layers. The last processing layer is already serving as the output.

The sequence of processing sizes three, two, four and five has three hidden groups. Adding a new three-neuron group before the last layer increases the hidden-layer count while keeping five output categories.

contrasts.title: A nonlinear step changes what a stack of weighted sums can represent.

left.text: A chain of **linear transformations** can be combined into one linear transformation. More such layers alone do not supply a nonlinear boundary.

right.text: **Sigmoid** changes each weighted sum through an S-shaped function. Applying it between layers makes the combined processing nonlinear.

paragraphs: The distinction concerns the operations, not just the number of neurons. A nonlinear transformation changes what later layers receive and must be carried through the remaining computation.
Keeping the original formants while inserting sigmoid changes the later activations and probabilities. That processing change is separate from an optimizer learning new weights.

contrasts.title: Being bounded is different from forming a category distribution.

left.text: Each **sigmoid activation** is between zero and one. Several such values are not required to add to one.

right.text: A **probability distribution** is also nonnegative but must sum to one across the specified alternatives.

paragraphs: The shared numerical range does not give the two representations the same job. Normalization across alternatives supplies a condition that separate hidden activations lack.
Three hidden values near one can be perfectly valid sigmoid activations. They would fail as three mutually exclusive category probabilities because their total would exceed one.

contrasts.title: Loss and accuracy describe different aspects of a prediction.

left.text: **Loss** quantifies mismatch with the training target. Its change can guide parameter updates.

right.text: **Accuracy** counts the fraction of category decisions that are correct. It does not fully describe the confidence assigned to each answer.

paragraphs: Two predictions can choose the same category while assigning it different support. Their accuracy can agree even though their losses differ.
A flat accuracy segment does not establish that every parameter or probability stayed fixed. The decision can remain unchanged while the model’s numerical support shifts.

contrasts.title: Performance on the training rows does not establish performance on new recordings.

left.text: **Training accuracy** measures decisions on the examples used in the displayed training setup.

right.text: **Generalization** concerns decisions on new examples. It requires evidence beyond the training rows.

paragraphs: The source run supports a claim about the supplied data and procedure. It cannot by itself establish the same percentage for new speakers or a different recording condition.
Overlapping categories help explain why the measured formants can be difficult to classify. A new-speaker evaluation would address a different question from whether training accuracy improved.

contrasts.title: Parallel heads and successive layers add different kinds of processing.

left.text: **Heads operate alongside one another within a layer**, contributing information about different relationships.

right.text: **Layers operate successively through depth**, transforming representations that already contain earlier processing.

paragraphs: Adding a parallel contribution is different from adding another stage after the existing one. The diagram uses both arrangements rather than treating them as interchangeable counts.
Several heads can contribute to one layer’s representation. The next layer then receives the combined result rather than merely acting as one more head in the same stage.

contrasts.title: A head works inside a model, while an agent carries out a task within a larger system.

left.text: An **attention head** is a computational component within a model layer. Its contribution is combined with other internal processing.

right.text: An **agent** is a model given a role and connected to other tasks through messages. A critic and reviser are roles in that larger organization.

paragraphs: A checking loop between models should not be described as just another attention head. The system-level graph and the model’s internal layers are different levels of explanation.
A critic can ask for a draft to be revised before it is returned. That message exchange is outside the individual model’s hidden activation calculations.

contrasts.title: A spelling prediction can probe a pattern without being a phonetic transcription.

left.text: **Letters** are written symbols. Their sequences can provide a practical word-completion exercise.

right.text: **Speech sounds** are the units articulated and heard. Their sequence restrictions are not identical to every spelling pattern.

paragraphs: The next-letter game can expose useful regularities while still requiring care about what is being represented. A written symbol does not always correspond to a pronounced consonant.
Written k can begin knee, but ordinary pronunciation does not begin with /k/. That example should not be used to claim that the spoken onset /kn/ is permitted in the same way.

hard.title: Why can a still point matter more for stiffness than a moving point?
paragraphs: A mode pattern describes **motion over a complete cycle**, not merely whether one dot happens to be at the center at a particular instant. A displacement node stays still throughout that cycle, while an antinode moves through a large range.

Stiffness concerns deformation between neighboring parts. Those neighbors can move strongly relative to one another around a node, so the node can coincide with strong spring action even though its own displacement is zero.

Adding mass at an antinode increases inertia where the mode already has substantial motion. Adding stiffness at a strongly deformed location increases the restoring action, so the two changes act on different spatial properties.

In the source’s marked-location comparison, one mode moves there and another has a node there. **Read the role in each mode first**, then predict a decrease from inertia or an increase from stiffness.
hard.question: Does a point momentarily crossing its resting position have to be a displacement node?
hard.answer: No. An antinode passes through the resting position during every cycle. **A node remains stationary through the entire mode**, which is a different condition.

hard.title: Why does the fixed–free series skip the even multiples?
paragraphs: Begin with the two endpoint requirements. One end must stay still, and the other must reach the maximum displacement allowed by the mode.
The shortest piece connecting those requirements is **one quarter-wave**. Adding another quarter-wave would bring the pattern back to a still point at the free end, violating that end’s condition.

Adding two quarter-waves instead brings the pattern back to a moving end. The permitted counts are therefore one, three, five and further odd counts, which produce the ideal odd-multiple frequency series.
This explains the series from the shape rather than treating it as an arbitrary list. A string held still at both ends has another constraint and can fit every whole number of half-waves.
hard.question: What is the first thing to check before assigning a harmonic series to a drawing?
hard.answer: Check **what each end is allowed to do**. The permitted spatial patterns depend on those conditions.

hard.title: How can a wave-shaped air diagram represent longitudinal motion?
paragraphs: The air particles move **along the vocal tract**. A graph can nevertheless draw their displacement vertically so that the size of the motion at each tube position is easy to see.
The drawing is a representation of a quantity, not a literal path through the roof and floor of the mouth. A large vertical value means large longitudinal displacement at that location.

Compression depends on how neighboring particles move relative to one another. Particles on either side of a small-displacement region can crowd together or spread apart strongly, producing pressure changes there.

Keeping displacement and compression separate makes the vowel predictions understandable. A narrowing can slow a moving region through inertia or raise a compressing mode’s frequency through increased stiffness.
hard.question: Why is the highest point on a displacement curve not automatically the point of greatest compression?
hard.answer: Its height describes **particle displacement**, while compression describes changing separation between neighbors. Those quantities have different spatial patterns.

hard.title: Why can the same vowel filter look different at different pitches?
paragraphs: A tract resonance describes a frequency region the filter favors. The source supplies only the harmonics available at its current F0, so those harmonics sample the filter’s response at discrete frequencies.

At low F0, closely spaced harmonics can fall on both sides of a resonance and reveal its broad envelope. At high F0, the next harmonic can lie far away, leaving a formant between the available samples.
The filter has not automatically lost its resonance when that region is poorly sampled. **The source pattern and the filter response are separate contributors** to the observed spectrum.

That distinction explains both the source-filter relationship and why some very high-pitched vowels are less clear. It also prevents a harmonic’s frequency from being mistaken for the exact location of a formant.
hard.question: Does the strongest visible harmonic always give the exact formant frequency?
hard.answer: No. It can be the available source harmonic nearest a resonance. **The resonance can lie between harmonics**.

hard.title: Why does working backward solve a forward network’s learning problem?
paragraphs: The forward computation creates the values needed for a prediction. Comparing that prediction with the target supplies an error, but it does not yet identify how each earlier connection contributed.
A final connection lies close to the error. An earlier connection acts through several later activations, so its effect depends on calculations that lie downstream from it.
**Backpropagation solves those downstream dependencies first and reuses them**. This is why dynamic programming is a useful explanation of its efficiency rather than an unrelated shortest-path story.

The reverse pass calculates gradients from the stored forward values. The optimizer then uses those gradients to update the parameters, keeping the order of calculation distinct from the act of changing weights.
hard.question: Are the final-layer weights repeatedly changed before each earlier gradient is calculated?
hard.answer: The backward calculation uses the forward-pass values and the current parameters to obtain consistent gradients. **The parameter update follows that calculation**, rather than rebuilding each earlier gradient from an already changed network.

hard.title: Why is “increase the weight” not a complete prediction?
paragraphs: A connection contributes the incoming activation multiplied by its weight. The sign of the activation therefore matters before the effect of increasing the weight can be determined.

For a positive activation entering a direct output connection, increasing the weight raises that output’s raw score. For a negative activation, the same weight increase pushes its contribution in the opposite direction.
Whether that direction helps also depends on the target. An output receiving too much support should be reduced, while an output receiving too little support needs a different correction.

For an early hidden connection, the change then passes through additional pathways and transformations. **Follow the sign, the target and the downstream dependencies**, rather than treating every increase as improvement.
hard.question: Which condition makes increasing a direct output weight raise that output’s raw score?
hard.answer: The incoming activation must be **positive**, with the other contributions held fixed. Its sign determines the local direction.

hard.title: Why do four Linear declarations correspond to three hidden layers?
paragraphs: The two input values are supplied measurements. They do not require a Linear declaration merely to exist as inputs.
Each Linear declaration creates a processing layer. In the displayed sequence, three layers produce intermediate activations and the last produces values for five vowel categories.
Only the intermediate layers are **hidden layers**. Counting the final decision layer as hidden would count one processing stage in the wrong category.

Inserting three neurons immediately before the output requires a four-to-three connection and then a three-to-five connection. The sizes must match where the layers meet, while the original two input measurements remain unchanged.
hard.question: Does adding a hidden layer require adding another measured formant input?
hard.answer: No. It adds an **internal processing stage**. The original input can remain F1 and F2.

hard.title: Why is a bounded activation not automatically a probability distribution?
paragraphs: Sigmoid maps one weighted sum to a number between zero and one. Applying it independently to several neurons gives several bounded numbers.
A distribution over mutually exclusive categories has another requirement. **The category probabilities must sum to one together**, which independent sigmoid activations do not ensure.
The hidden values can be useful features without being category decisions. Their job is to supply a representation for the next processing stage.
Sigmoid also introduces nonlinearity between weighted combinations. That changes the function being calculated and requires later activations to be recomputed from the transformed values.
hard.question: Can three hidden sigmoid neurons all be close to one?
hard.answer: Yes. Their activations are independently bounded. **Their sum is not constrained to one**, because they are not automatically alternative-category probabilities.

hard.title: Why can a cluster work inside a word but fail at the beginning of a syllable?
paragraphs: Sound restrictions apply to positions within syllables, not merely to an uninterrupted row of written consonants. A syllable has an onset before its vowel and a coda after it.

A consonant sequence inside a longer word can span a syllable boundary. The first consonant can finish one syllable while the next begins another, avoiding a combination that would be disallowed in a single onset.

The next-letter exercise makes some of these expectations visible by restricting the continuation of a word beginning. A model that predicts well must become sensitive to which completions fit the available context.

**Letters still differ from sounds**, so spelling examples such as knee need careful interpretation. They can probe written pattern knowledge without establishing that every written cluster is pronounced as an onset.
hard.question: Why should a written k followed by n not be treated as proof of a spoken /kn/ onset?
hard.answer: Ordinary knee does not pronounce that initial written k. **The spelling sequence and the pronounced sound sequence are different representations**.

connections.title: The free top of a building helps explain loading near the lips.
paragraphs: A building is constrained at its base while its top can move. The neutral vocal-tract model gives its air column a corresponding **closed end and open end**, making the endpoint relationship useful despite the different materials.
Adding moving mass at the free top slows the building mode in the ideal comparison. Loading the strongly moving lip region similarly lowers the first two resonances in the /u/ model.
The explanation transfers **where the load acts within the mode**. It does not require air to bend sideways or every real building to have the same resonance ratios as a uniform tube.
connections.question: Why would moving the load away from the free end require a new prediction?
connections.answer: The new position can have different motion and deformation in each mode. **The endpoint conclusion cannot simply be copied to another location**.

connections.title: A physical speech mechanism can become information for a classifier.
paragraphs: Vocal-fold vibration supplies the periodic source, and the vocal tract shapes its harmonic strengths. Measuring the resulting sound gives information about the tract resonances.
**F1 and F2 become numerical inputs** to the vowel network. The classifier then uses learned weights to turn those measurements into support for the possible categories.
The measurement is not itself a category label. A tract configuration, an acoustic representation and a network decision are different stages connected by a causal and computational path.
connections.question: Why can an F1–F2 measurement be sensible even when the network labels it incorrectly?
connections.answer: The physical measurement and the learned decision have different roles. **Poor weights can misclassify a valid measurement**.

connections.title: A mode mixture connects visible motion with a spectrum.
paragraphs: Several normal modes can contribute to the movement recorded at one location. Their superposition can produce a complex time trace even when each component pattern is organized.
A spectrum separates contributions by frequency. **The complex trace and its frequency components describe the same combined signal** in different representations.
The contribution of a mode also depends on where the measurement is taken. A point that is a node for one component cannot display strong motion from that component.
connections.question: Why can a single pickup fail to reveal one mode strongly?
connections.answer: The pickup can lie near that mode’s **displacement node**, where its contribution to the local movement is small.

connections.title: A frequency shift can reveal what a location was doing.
paragraphs: A forward prediction starts with the local role and predicts the direction of change. A motion-dominated region responds strongly to added inertia, while a compression-dominated region responds strongly to stiffness.
The reasoning can also be used in reverse. **A large upward resonance shift points toward a dominant restoring-stiffness effect** at the changed location for that mode.
The inference stays mode-specific because another mode can use the same location differently. A result about F2 should not be silently generalized to F1.
connections.question: What would a downward shift suggest under the same constriction model?
connections.answer: It suggests that the **motion-related inertial effect dominates** for that mode at that location.

connections.title: Speech recognition and sequence prediction both benefit from context.
paragraphs: A following vowel can carry information about a preceding consonant. The splice example therefore makes clear that the relevant evidence extends beyond a narrowly isolated segment.
A sequence model likewise uses context when deciding a continuation. **Relations among items can contribute information that no single item supplies alone**.
The two cases illustrate the value of context at different levels. The splice result does not establish that human speech perception implements a particular language-model architecture.
connections.question: What is lost when every input fragment is classified independently?
connections.answer: The system loses **relationships across fragments**, including transitions and contextual restrictions that can help resolve an identity.

connections.title: A downstream error calculation resembles a reusable route value.
paragraphs: A shortest-path value summarizes a solved continuation that many earlier routes can use. Calculating that same continuation independently for each path would repeat work.

An early neural connection also depends on downstream computations. **Backpropagation solves and reuses those dependencies** instead of independently tracing every full route from every early parameter to the error.
The shared principle is dynamic programming over dependent calculations. The numerical quantity in the network is a derivative of loss, rather than the distance remaining on a road.
connections.question: Why is the comparison useful even though a derivative is not a route cost?
connections.answer: Both problems can reuse **shared solved subproblems**. The organizational relationship transfers without making the two quantities identical.

connections.title: Current activations and learned weights contribute different kinds of information.
paragraphs: Activations express the values being processed for the current input and context. Weights determine how those values influence the next computation.
A recurrent state can carry information between steps without replacing every learned connection. **What is currently being processed differs from the parameters that organize processing**.

Learning changes parameters using feedback, while ordinary inference can change activations repeatedly with the parameters held fixed. This distinction remains useful as a model becomes deeper or processes longer sequences.
connections.question: Does a different activation pattern prove that learning occurred?
connections.answer: No. A new input or context can change activations during **inference with unchanged weights**.

connections.title: Repeated transformation links physical dynamics with network depth.
paragraphs: A physical oscillator repeatedly updates its state through time. A deep model repeatedly transforms its representations as they pass through processing layers.
Both accounts require identifying **the current state and the rule producing the next state**. This makes a changing numerical representation easier to understand as a process.
The analogy has limits because different network layers can have different weights. Repeated transformation does not require a literal physical oscillator or one identical matrix reused everywhere.
connections.question: What remains useful when the rule differs from layer to layer?
connections.answer: The idea that **the output representation of one step becomes the input state of the next** remains useful.

connections.title: Next-letter practice gives a small example of learning from completion.
paragraphs: A word beginning limits which letters can plausibly follow. Correctly predicting the next letter therefore requires sensitivity to patterns already present in the sequence.

A model can learn from the gap between its predicted distribution and the actual continuation. **Completion makes language regularities available as training information** without providing a separate verbal explanation of every rule.

The representation still matters. Written-letter patterns can reflect spelling as well as sound structure, so successful completion should be interpreted in relation to what the model actually receives.
connections.question: Why is a broad next-letter distribution sometimes appropriate?
connections.answer: Some contexts allow many plausible continuations. **Knowledge can support uncertainty**, rather than always requiring one sharply favored answer.

connections.title: A critic-and-reviser loop adds feedback at the system level.
paragraphs: An agentic system can assign drafting and checking to different models. Feedback from the critic then changes the next revision rather than being discarded after the first response.
**The loop operates between task-performing models**, while attention heads and hidden layers operate inside a model. Keeping those levels separate makes the diagram’s organization clear.
A checking process can improve an answer but still requires evidence about what it caught. The presence of a critic is a procedure, not a guarantee that every remaining statement is true.
connections.question: How could the checking process be evaluated?
connections.answer: Compare its claims with **independent source evidence** and check whether the revisions actually resolved the identified problems.

figures.title: Compare cycle rates over the same interval.
figures.takeaway: **The slower row is the heavier system**, and the faster row is the stiffer system in the controlled comparison. The size of the drawn movement is a separate feature from the number of cycles.

figures.title: Read a shared-direction pattern and an opposing-direction pattern.
figures.takeaway: **Opposing movement stretches the middle coupling more strongly**. The combined row adds the two patterns rather than introducing a third independent normal mode.

figures.title: Locate the stationary middle mass in the second mode.
figures.takeaway: **Mode 2 leaves the middle mass still**, even while the outer masses move. Modes 1 and 3 use its motion, which is why middle-mass loading affects their frequencies.

figures.title: Separate the number of masses from the number of the mode.
figures.takeaway: **A row with more moving masses permits more independent mode patterns**. The column identifies a particular mode rather than a new object being added to the same system.

figures.title: Fit half-wave pieces between two still endpoints.
figures.takeaway: **Every complete half-wave count preserves the two fixed ends**. The source animation’s construction explains the harmonic spacing instead of reducing it to an unexplained list of frequencies.

figures.title: Follow more than one spatial direction on a vibrating surface.
figures.takeaway: **A pickup records the combined local contribution of the modes**. A point at a node for a component will not move strongly because of that component.

figures.title: Fit quarter-wave pieces without turning the free end into a node.
figures.takeaway: **One, three, five and further odd quarter-wave counts** end at the required moving point. The original construction animation remains available, including where its static slide export is incomplete.

figures.title: Distinguish longitudinal air movement from its plotted representation.
figures.takeaway: **The vertical curve records displacement size at each tract location**. It does not mean that the air particles physically travel upward and downward through the tract walls.

figures.title: Connect tongue and lip configurations with the narrowed region.
figures.takeaway: **The position of the narrowing differs across vowels**, so the two air modes encounter it in different roles. The anatomical image supplies the tract configuration, while the mode model supplies its acoustic interpretation.

figures.title: Inspect the same boxed location in both mode patterns.
figures.takeaway: **One mode moves strongly in the box while the other is spring-dominated there**. Local loading therefore has to be interpreted twice, once for each mode.

figures.title: Read the lip-region loading in both first modes.
figures.takeaway: **Both modes have strong motion near the lips**, so the inertial effect lowers both frequencies. The result is a causal explanation of low F1 and F2 in this comparison.

figures.title: Use one constriction location to explain opposite shifts.
figures.takeaway: **Mode 1 is motion-dominated and Mode 2 compression-dominated** at the illustrated /i/ narrowing. The two formant directions follow from those different local roles.

figures.title: Check how a different narrowing reverses the first two roles.
figures.takeaway: **Compression dominates the first mode while motion dominates the second** at the /a/ location. F1 therefore rises while F2 falls in the source comparison.

figures.title: Read the source peaks as a regular harmonic comb.
figures.takeaway: **Higher F0 leaves wider gaps between peaks in the same frequency window**. It changes the sampling available to the tract filter rather than redefining each peak as a formant.

figures.title: Compare the source comb with the shaped neutral-vowel envelope.
figures.takeaway: **The harmonic frequency positions remain tied to the source**, while their heights follow the filter response. The broad envelope supplies information about the tract resonances.

figures.title: Recognize the low first formant and high second formant of /i/.
figures.takeaway: **The envelope favors separated low-F1 and high-F2 regions**. Several source harmonics can contribute near each resonance, so a formant is not one isolated numbered harmonic.

figures.title: Compare the closer first and second formants of /a/.
figures.takeaway: **The first two favored frequency regions lie closer together than in the /i/ comparison**. Their positions connect with the different tract constriction rather than a changed definition of F0.

figures.title: Keep source-row changes separate from filter-column changes.
figures.takeaway: **Rows change the source’s harmonic spacing and columns change the vowel filter**. The grid is useful because it varies those two contributions separately.

figures.title: Follow frequency bands through time instead of reading height as loudness.
figures.takeaway: **The rising first band and falling second band track the /i/ to /a/ transition**. Darkness records amplitude, while the bands’ vertical position records frequency.

figures.title: Count the hidden groups and follow the incoming connections.
figures.takeaway: **The three internal groups contain three, two and four neurons**. Each receiving neuron has one incoming weight for each value in the preceding group.

figures.title: Connect the same two input measurements with the final category decision.
figures.takeaway: **The displayed network favors done although the target is dean**. The mismatch separates completing a valid forward calculation from having learned an accurate classifier.

figures.title: Compare a marked final connection with a marked early connection.
figures.takeaway: **The final connection has a more direct route to the output error**. The early connection’s effect is mediated by the remaining activations and weights.

figures.title: Keep each formant row aligned with its target row.
figures.takeaway: **The input table describes measurements and the target table identifies categories**. A one in the dean column belongs to the recording classified as dean, not to whichever input happens to occupy that row after an independent shuffle.

figures.title: Read the middle and extremes of the S-shaped response.
figures.takeaway: **A weighted sum near zero produces a middle activation**, while large magnitudes approach the bounds. The curve’s slope explains why an equal input change can have different output effects at different locations.

figures.title: Distinguish the original weighted sum from the transformed hidden response.
figures.takeaway: **The transformed value must be used by downstream connections**. Leaving the later values unchanged would no longer describe the network with sigmoid applied.

figures.title: Read each point as one labeled vowel token.
figures.takeaway: **The horizontal and vertical coordinates are F1 and F2**, while the category marking identifies the vowel. Overlap means nearby measured values can belong to different categories.

figures.title: Read accuracy as a proportion of correct training decisions.
figures.takeaway: **The curve rises from around the five-category guessing baseline and plateaus at 44.95 percent**. Its axes describe progress over updates and training accuracy, not how loud or clear the vowels were.

figures.title: Compare different paths and a shared endpoint.
figures.takeaway: **All displayed runs reach the same final training accuracy despite different early curves**. The result separates variability in the route from variability in the final proportion correct.

figures.title: Locate the information passed between processing steps.
figures.takeaway: **Feedback carries context into the next computation**. A recurrent state is not simply another independent classification of an isolated input.

figures.title: Read horizontal parallel work separately from vertical depth.
figures.takeaway: **Several heads contribute within one layer**, then the representation moves to a successive layer. Counting heads and counting layers answers different architectural questions.

figures.title: Follow a changing representation through repeated processing.
figures.takeaway: **An output representation becomes an input to a later transformation**. The connection to dynamics concerns this repeated change rather than literal motion of the model’s internal numbers.

figures.title: Keep the representation and next-item task separate.
figures.takeaway: **The input items are represented as vectors even when their original materials differ**. Context across the sequence determines which continuation the model should favor.

figures.title: Compare a valid onset with a cluster divided by a syllable boundary.
figures.takeaway: **Position within the syllable changes which sequences are allowed**. A consonant cluster in the middle of a word does not automatically establish the same cluster as a possible word beginning.

figures.title: Read a restriction on continuations as information in the context.
figures.takeaway: **Some beginnings allow many letters while others leave a narrow set of choices**. Their probability distributions should differ accordingly rather than treating every uncertain context as equally unconstrained.

figures.title: Separate the levels from one neuron to a graph of communicating models.
figures.takeaway: **A model’s internal processing differs from messages between task-performing models**. The critic-to-reviser connection belongs to the larger system’s organization.

asked.title: Count the modes and explain their motion.

items.question: How many normal modes can a three-mass system support in the one-direction model?
items.answer: **Three**. Each independent moving mass adds one degree of freedom, giving three independent normal-mode patterns.

items.question: Which of the three modes has the highest frequency, and what makes it faster?
items.answer: **Mode 3** has the highest frequency. Neighboring masses alternate in direction, producing stronger restoring action than the broad shared motion of the lowest mode.

items.question: What happens to Mode 2 if only the middle mass is made heavier?
items.answer: Its frequency stays unchanged in the ideal symmetric system. **The middle mass does not move in Mode 2**, so the added inertia does not contribute to that mode.

asked.title: Decide what matters at a marked location.

items.question: A marked point moves strongly in one mode but stays still in another. Will added mass affect both modes equally?
items.answer: No. It lowers the frequency of the mode with substantial motion there and has no effect at an exact displacement node. **The effect depends on local participation in each mode**.

items.question: Why can extra stiffness at a stationary point still change a mode’s frequency?
items.answer: The point can lie where neighboring regions deform strongly even though its own displacement is zero. **Stiffness responds to deformation**, not to the size of the local displacement alone.

items.question: If the same change raises one resonance and lowers another, must the measurements be inconsistent?
items.answer: No. The changed location can be dominated by compression in one mode and motion in the other. Those different local roles allow opposite frequency shifts.

asked.title: Fit the boundary conditions before naming the frequencies.

items.question: A uniform string is fixed at both ends and has a 200 Hz fundamental. What frequency is its fifth mode?
items.answer: **1,000 Hz**. The ideal fixed-at-both-ends string has whole-number harmonics, so its fifth mode is five times the fundamental.

items.question: Why does the second mode of a fixed-at-both-ends string have a shorter wavelength than the first?
items.answer: It fits two half-waves into the length that held one half-wave. **More wave pieces in the same distance mean a shorter wavelength** and, at the same wave speed, a higher frequency.

items.question: Which frequencies belong in a spectrum through the first six modes when the fundamental is 200 Hz?
items.answer: **200, 400, 600, 800, 1,000 and 1,200 Hz**. The peaks remain evenly spaced by the fundamental.

asked.title: Explain why the two different ends permit odd multiples.

items.question: What would go wrong if an even number of quarter-waves were fitted between a fixed end and a free end?
items.answer: The pattern would reach a still point at the free end instead of a point of greatest displacement. **The boundary conditions would no longer match**.

items.question: Why is a building a useful analogy for the end constraints of a vocal tract?
items.answer: A building is held at its base and free at its top. A neutral vocal-tract air column likewise has different constraints at the glottal and lip ends, making **fixed–free organization** the shared feature.

items.question: For an ideal fixed–free tube with a 500 Hz first resonance, what are the next two resonances?
items.answer: **1,500 Hz and 2,500 Hz**. The ideal neutral tube supports odd multiples of its lowest resonance.

asked.title: Keep the fundamental and its harmonics distinct.

items.question: A periodic voice has F0 at 150 Hz. Where are its first five harmonic peaks?
items.answer: **150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz**. Harmonics occur at whole-number multiples of the source’s repetition frequency.

items.question: What happens to harmonic spacing if the vocal folds vibrate faster?
items.answer: **The spacing increases**. The fundamental is the repetition rate, and it is also the separation between adjacent source harmonics.

items.question: Does the third harmonic have to be the third formant?
items.answer: No. **A harmonic belongs to the periodic source**, while **a formant is a tract resonance**. Their numbering refers to different sequences.

asked.title: Infer the constriction’s effect from the mode pattern.

items.question: A constriction raises F2 strongly. Was the air mostly moving or compressing at that location in Mode 2?
items.answer: **Compression was the stronger effect**. Increasing restoring stiffness where the mode compresses raises its frequency.

items.question: Why does narrowing the tract not always raise every formant?
items.answer: A narrowing also changes effective inertia. **At a strongly moving location, inertial loading can dominate and lower a formant**, even while stiffness increases locally.

items.question: What extra information is needed before predicting whether a local tract change raises F1?
items.answer: The location of the change within the **first mode’s motion and compression pattern** is needed. The fact that a narrowing occurred does not by itself determine the direction.

asked.title: Explain the opposing F1 and F2 directions.

items.question: How can one front constriction lower F1 while raising F2?
items.answer: It falls in a region dominated by motion for the first mode and compression for the second. **The inertial effect lowers F1 and the stiffness effect raises F2**.

items.question: Which illustrated vowel change lowers both first and second formants, and why?
items.answer: The **/u/ model** loads the region near the lips. Both of the first two modes have strong motion there, so increased inertial loading lowers both frequencies.

items.question: Why does moving a constriction toward the /a/ location reverse the /i/ pattern?
items.answer: The first two modes have different local roles at the new location. **Compression dominates Mode 1 while motion dominates Mode 2**, so F1 rises and F2 falls.

asked.title: Describe what the source supplies and the filter changes.

items.question: What changes when the same voiced source is filtered as /i/ and then /a/?
items.answer: The **formant pattern and the relative harmonic amplitudes** change as the tract shape changes. The source’s harmonic spacing can remain the same.

items.question: Why can a formant be present even when no harmonic lies exactly at its frequency?
items.answer: A formant is a property of the tract’s resonant response. **The source samples that response only at its available harmonic frequencies**, so a resonance need not coincide with a harmonic.

items.question: Why can high-pitched singing make a vowel harder to identify?
items.answer: High F0 spreads the harmonics farther apart. Fewer peaks may sample the formant envelope, making the intended resonance pattern less clear.

asked.title: Read what the acoustic display encodes.

items.question: What does a dark region high on a spectrogram represent?
items.answer: It represents **relatively strong energy at a high frequency** at that time. Height encodes frequency and darkness encodes amplitude.

items.question: How would a transition from /i/ toward /a/ appear in the first two formant bands?
items.answer: **F1 would rise and F2 would fall** toward the /a/ pattern. The bands would change through time rather than merely become darker in place.

items.question: What information does a spectrum alone leave out that a spectrogram provides?
items.answer: A spectrum describes one time window. **A spectrogram preserves the sequence of changing frequency patterns**, allowing transitions to be followed.

asked.title: Explain the order of the backward calculation.

items.question: Why is the effect of a final-layer weight easier to connect to the error than the effect of an early weight?
items.answer: The final-layer weight has a short, direct route to the output. An early weight influences the error **through several intermediate activations and connections**.

items.question: How does dynamic programming help backpropagation avoid repeated work?
items.answer: Downstream error calculations are solved first and reused when calculating earlier effects. **Shared dependent computations do not have to be rebuilt independently for each weight**.

items.question: Does calculating a gradient itself complete an SGD weight update?
items.answer: No. **Backpropagation calculates the gradient**, and the optimizer applies a correction using that gradient and the learning rate.

asked.title: Trace a proposed weight change to its consequence.

items.question: A positive hidden activation feeds an output that already has too much support. What does increasing its direct output weight do?
items.answer: It raises that output’s raw score, which works against reducing its excessive support. **The sign of the incoming activation** makes the local direction predictable.

items.question: Would increasing the same connection necessarily have the same effect if its input activation were negative?
items.answer: No. Multiplying a negative activation by a larger weight changes the contribution in the opposite direction. **The input sign must be considered along with the weight**.

items.question: Why should an early hidden weight not be judged only from the sign printed beside it?
items.answer: Its final effect passes through later connections and nonlinear transformations. **The downstream pathways determine how the change reaches the error**.

asked.title: Read layer sizes and adjust the network coherently.

items.question: How many hidden layers are in a network with processing sizes 3, 2, 4 and 5, where five neurons provide the output?
items.answer: **Three hidden layers**. The final five-neuron layer is the output layer, while the supplied two-value input is not another hidden layer.

items.question: What does nn.Linear(3, 2) specify?
items.answer: It receives **three values** and produces **two activations** through learned weighted combinations. The following processing layer must accept those two outputs.

items.question: Which two connections are needed to insert three hidden neurons between four hidden activations and five outputs?
items.answer: Use a connection from **four to three**, followed by a connection from **three to five**. That inserts the hidden layer while preserving the five output categories.

asked.title: Recognize what the training operations accomplish.

items.question: Why must the row order agree between formant inputs and vowel targets?
items.answer: Each pair describes the same recording. **A mismatched row teaches an incorrect formant-to-vowel association**, even if both tables have valid numerical entries.

items.question: What does loss.backward() contribute before the optimizer takes a step?
items.answer: It computes how the loss depends on the trainable parameters. **Those gradients supply the directions and strengths used by the update**.

items.question: What is the effect of increasing the learning rate while leaving the gradients unchanged?
items.answer: **The parameter steps become larger**. That can speed movement but can also increase instability or fluctuation.

asked.title: Explain the nonlinear transformation without evaluating exponentials.

items.question: What does sigmoid do to a very negative weighted sum?
items.answer: It produces an activation **close to zero**. A very positive sum instead produces a value close to one.

items.question: Why does sigmoid change the function of a stack of linear layers?
items.answer: It adds a nonlinear transformation between the weighted combinations. **The resulting network can no longer be collapsed into one purely linear transformation** in the same way.

items.question: Why are three hidden sigmoid values not automatically probabilities over three categories?
items.answer: They are individually bounded, but **they are not required to sum to one**. Being in the probability range is only one condition of a category distribution.

asked.title: Interpret the training curve and repeated runs.

items.question: Why is twenty percent a useful guessing baseline for five equally likely categories?
items.answer: A uniform guess has **one chance in five** of selecting the correct category. The baseline follows from the number and balance of the choices.

items.question: Does a flat training-accuracy curve mean that every example is classified correctly?
items.answer: No. A plateau only indicates that the measured proportion is no longer increasing. **A stable result can still contain many incorrect decisions**.

items.question: What remains different when runs start with different weights but finish at the same accuracy?
items.answer: **Their learning paths can differ**. Early predictions and corrections depend on initialization even when the eventual proportion correct agrees.

asked.title: Transfer the sequence-prediction idea across different materials.

items.question: What do words and a sequence of acoustic measurements have in common for a numerical predictor?
items.answer: Both can be represented as **ordered vectors**. The model uses the preceding vectors to predict a continuation, although the representation and output interpretation differ.

items.question: Why can an isolated word be insufficient to decide the next word?
items.answer: Its continuation depends on the broader sequence. **Earlier context changes which next items fit**, so independent item classification leaves out useful information.

items.question: What does a recurrent connection contribute to a sequence model?
items.answer: It carries state from one processing step into another. **The current computation can therefore depend on prior context**, rather than only the current input.

asked.title: Use a changed word beginning to reason about a continuation.

items.question: Why is n a poor next-letter choice after initial sp in the supplied English pattern exercise?
items.answer: It would create the excluded **spn onset pattern**. A vowel, l or r fits the illustrated alternatives.

items.question: Why can a consonant sequence occur inside a longer word but fail as a word beginning?
items.answer: A syllable break can divide the consonants between different positions. **Allowed sequences depend on syllable structure**, so a cross-boundary cluster need not be a permitted onset.

items.question: How should a predictor’s distribution differ between a highly restricted beginning and a permissive one?
items.answer: The restricted beginning should concentrate support on fewer continuations. The permissive beginning allows a **broader distribution** over plausible next items.

asked.title: Distinguish the organization within a model from a system of models.

items.question: Are several attention heads in one layer the same as several successive processing layers?
items.answer: No. **Heads work in parallel within a layer**, while successive layers transform representations through depth.

items.question: Why is a critic-to-reviser loop a kind of feedback?
items.answer: The critic’s evaluation returns information that changes another processing attempt. **The later result depends on feedback from an earlier result**.

items.question: Does calling a head an expert guarantee that it understands a topic as a person does?
items.answer: No. The analogy describes a specialized computational contribution. It does not establish a human-like role or a separately verifiable area of expertise.
